```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = FALSE)
```

When your R code calls a hosted language model, the work happens in the
provider's datacenter. CodeCarbon measures the electricity *your machine*
draws, so it cannot see it. A **remote tracker** estimates that provider-side
impact instead, and it goes wherever a CodeCarbon tracker goes:
`carbon_track()`, `carbon_track_all()`, `carbon_run()`, `carbon_step()` and
`tracker_start()` / `tracker_stop()`.

This guide classifies the sentiment of eight product reviews with
`openai/gpt-6-luna` and tracks what the requests cost. The output shown is
from a real run.

## Setup

You need [ellmer](https://ellmer.tidyverse.org) and an API key. This guide
reaches the model through OpenRouter. Put the key in a `.env` file in your
project folder, with no spaces around the `=`, and keep that file out of
version control:

```
OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-...
```

Then load it with `readRenviron()`:

```{r}
library(tidycarbon)
library(ellmer)
library(dplyr)

readRenviron(".env")
```

A key already set in `~/.Renviron` works too, without the `readRenviron()`
call. With an OpenAI key, use `chat_openai(model = "gpt-6-luna")` instead;
everything else is identical.

## The task

```{r}
reviews <- c(
  "Absolutely love this kettle, boils in under a minute.",
  "Stopped working after two weeks. Very disappointed.",
  "It does what it says. Nothing more, nothing less.",
  "The battery life is incredible, I charge it once a week.",
  "Customer service never replied to my emails.",
  "Arrived on time and matches the description.",
  "Far too loud for a bedroom fan, I sent it back.",
  "Best purchase I have made all year!"
)

system_prompt <- "You classify the sentiment of product reviews."

new_chat <- function() {
  chat_openrouter(
    model = "openai/gpt-6-luna",
    system_prompt = system_prompt,
    echo = "none"
  )
}

# One numbered line per review, so all eight go in a single request.
numbered <- function(texts) paste0(seq_along(texts), ". ", texts, collapse = "\n")

chat <- new_chat()

sentiment_type <- type_array(items = type_object(
  id        = type_integer("Number of the review"),
  sentiment = type_enum(values = c("positive", "neutral", "negative"))
))

classify <- function(texts) {
  chat$chat_structured(numbered(texts), type = sentiment_type)
}
```

## Create a remote tracker

Where `carbon_init()` creates a CodeCarbon tracker for your machine,
`carbon_init_remote()` creates one for the provider. Give it the chat your
code uses:

```{r}
tracker <- carbon_init_remote(chat, project_name = "sentiment")
```

The estimate comes from [EcoLogits](https://ecologits.ai), which is installed
automatically through reticulate.

Everything the tracker measures is also appended to `emissions_remote.csv`
in your working directory, one row per window. Change the location with
`output_dir` and `output_file`, or pass `output_dir = NULL` to write nothing.
Read it back with `carbon_read(".", "emissions_remote.csv")`.

## Track the classification

```{r}
res <- carbon_track(classify, texts = reviews, tracker = tracker)

res$result[[1]]
#>   id sentiment
#> 1  1  positive
#> 2  2  negative
#> 3  3   neutral
#> 4  4  positive
#> 5  5  negative
#> 6  6   neutral
#> 7  7  negative
#> 8  8  positive
```

`res` is one tidy row: the result, plus the estimate for the requests made
while `classify()` ran.

```{r}
res |>
  select(duration, n_calls, n_modelled, output_tokens, engine, engine_version)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 6
#>   duration n_calls n_modelled output_tokens engine    engine_version
#>      <dbl>   <int>      <int>         <dbl> <chr>     <chr>
#> 1     4.75       1          1           143 ecologits 0.11.2
```

The impact columns use CodeCarbon's names and units (`energy_consumed` in
kWh, `emissions_total` in kgCO2eq, `water_consumed` in L), each as a lower
and an upper bound:

```{r}
res |>
  transmute(
    energy_wh_min = energy_consumed_min * 1000,
    energy_wh_max = energy_consumed_max * 1000,
    co2e_mg_min   = emissions_total_min * 1e6,
    co2e_mg_max   = emissions_total_max * 1e6,
    water_ml_min  = water_consumed_min * 1000,
    water_ml_max  = water_consumed_max * 1000
  )
#> # A tibble: 1 × 6
#>   energy_wh_min energy_wh_max co2e_mg_min co2e_mg_max water_ml_min water_ml_max
#>           <dbl>         <dbl>       <dbl>       <dbl>        <dbl>        <dbl>
#> 1        0.0213        0.0227        9.59        10.1       0.0769       0.0820
```

It is a range because OpenAI does not publish the size of its models, so
EcoLogits brackets it. Each impact also has a `*_mean` column, the midpoint
of the range, for when you need a single figure.

## Look at the individual requests

The `calls` list-column holds one row per request:

```{r}
res$calls[[1]] |>
  select(provider, model, modelled, error,
         input_tokens, output_tokens, latency_s, grid_zone)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 8
#>   provider model             modelled error input_tokens output_tokens latency_s grid_zone
#>   <chr>    <chr>             <lgl>    <chr>        <dbl>         <dbl>     <dbl> <chr>
#> 1 openai   openai/gpt-6-luna TRUE     NA             187           143      4.75 USA
```

Always check `modelled`. A model EcoLogits has not registered, often one
newer than the installed release, is left out: `modelled = FALSE`, impacts
`NA`, and `error` holds the code `"model-not-registered"`. `n_modelled` in
the summary row counts the requests that were actually estimated.

## Compare two prompting strategies

Does asking the model to justify each label cost more? Track both versions
with `carbon_track_all()`. Each version gets its own chat, and one tracker
watches both:

```{r}
chat_reason <- new_chat()

reason_type <- type_array(items = type_object(
  id        = type_integer("Number of the review"),
  sentiment = type_enum(values = c("positive", "neutral", "negative")),
  reason    = type_string("One sentence explaining the label")
))

classify_reason <- function(texts) {
  chat_reason$chat_structured(numbered(texts), type = reason_type)
}

tracker <- carbon_init_remote(list(chat, chat_reason), project_name = "sentiment")

runs <- carbon_track_all(
  list(
    list(fun = classify,        args = list(texts = reviews)),
    list(fun = classify_reason, args = list(texts = reviews))
  ),
  tracker
)

runs |>
  mutate(strategy = c("label only", "label + reason")) |>
  transmute(strategy, n_calls, output_tokens,
            energy_wh_min = energy_consumed_min * 1000,
            energy_wh_max = energy_consumed_max * 1000)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 5
#>   strategy       n_calls output_tokens energy_wh_min energy_wh_max
#>   <chr>            <int>         <dbl>         <dbl>         <dbl>
#> 1 label only           1           133        0.0201        0.0214
#> 2 label + reason       1           280        0.0342        0.0370
```

The explanations double the output tokens, and the estimate rises by about
70%. Output length is what drives the estimate, so trimming what you
ask the model to write is the most direct way to lower it.

## Measure your machine and the provider together

`carbon_track()` takes one tracker. To cover the same code with both, give it
the CodeCarbon tracker and open the remote tracker's window around the call
with `tracker_start()` / `tracker_stop()`:

```{r}
local <- carbon_init(project_name = "sentiment", measure_power_secs = 1)

tracker_start(tracker)                 # provider window opens
res_local  <- carbon_track(classify, texts = reviews, tracker = local)
res_remote <- tracker_stop(tracker)    # provider window closes
```

Each tracker returns its own table. `res_local` is what your machine drew
while it waited for the answer:

```{r}
res_local |> select(duration, energy_consumed, emissions_total)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 3
#>   duration energy_consumed emissions_total
#>      <dbl>           <dbl>           <dbl>
#> 1     3.38       0.0000998       0.0000380
```

`res_remote` is the estimate for the requests made inside the window:

```{r}
res_remote |> select(n_calls, energy_consumed_min, energy_consumed_max)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 3
#>   n_calls energy_consumed_min energy_consumed_max
#>     <int>               <dbl>               <dbl>
#> 1       1           0.0000302           0.0000323
```

Both are in kWh, but do not add them. One is your whole machine, measured;
the other is the provider's datacenter, modelled.

## Without ellmer: a direct API call

A remote tracker reads its requests from an ellmer chat. With any other
client you do that step yourself: every provider's API reports the tokens it
billed, and that is all the estimate needs. Here is the first request again,
sent straight to OpenRouter's endpoint with
[httr2](https://httr2.r-lib.org):

```{r}
library(httr2)

started <- Sys.time()
resp <- request("https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions") |>
  req_auth_bearer_token(Sys.getenv("OPENROUTER_API_KEY")) |>
  req_body_json(list(
    model = "openai/gpt-6-luna",
    messages = list(
      list(role = "system", content = system_prompt),
      list(role = "user", content = numbered(reviews))
    )
  )) |>
  req_perform() |>
  resp_body_json()
latency <- as.numeric(difftime(Sys.time(), started, units = "secs"))
```

The response carries what the estimate needs: `resp$model` is the model that
answered and `resp$usage` the tokens billed. Put them in a calls table, one
row per request, with `carbon_calls()`:

```{r}
calls <- carbon_calls(
  model         = resp$model,
  provider      = "OpenRouter",
  output_tokens = resp$usage$completion_tokens,
  input_tokens  = resp$usage$prompt_tokens,
  latency_s     = latency
)
```

`carbon_provider()` estimates each row, and `carbon_provider_summary()` adds
them up:

```{r}
est <- carbon_provider(calls)

est |> select(provider, model, modelled, error, output_tokens, latency_s, grid_zone)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 7
#>   provider model             modelled error output_tokens latency_s grid_zone
#>   <chr>    <chr>             <lgl>    <chr>         <dbl>     <dbl> <chr>
#> 1 openai   openai/gpt-6-luna TRUE     NA               93      3.24 USA

carbon_provider_summary(est) |>
  select(calls, n_modelled, output_tokens,
         energy_kwh_min, energy_kwh_mean, energy_kwh_max)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 6
#>   calls n_modelled output_tokens energy_kwh_min energy_kwh_mean energy_kwh_max
#>   <int>      <int>         <dbl>          <dbl>           <dbl>          <dbl>
#> 1     1          1            93      0.0000146       0.0000151      0.0000155
```

This is the calculation a remote tracker runs for you. The plain-text answer
is shorter than the structured one (93 output tokens against 143), so the
estimate is lower too. Three things to get right when you do it by hand:

- **Name the provider.** With `"OpenRouter"`, the provider is read from the
  model id: `openai/gpt-6-luna` is estimated as OpenAI's `gpt-6-luna`. For a
  provider's own endpoint, use its EcoLogits id (`"openai"`, `"anthropic"`,
  `"mistralai"`, `"google_genai"`, `"cohere"`, `"huggingface_hub"`).
- **One row per request.** For several requests, pass vectors to
  `carbon_calls()`. Never sum the tokens first: the estimate is computed per
  request.
- **Latency is optional.** It can only lower the estimate, so leave it `NA`
  if you did not time the request.

## How to read the numbers

- **They are estimates, not measurements.** EcoLogits models inference from
  the model's size and the length of its output. Nothing is measured at the
  provider.
- **Only output tokens count.** The 187 input tokens above add nothing to the
  estimate, so a long prompt looks free.
- **The tracker sees only the chats you gave it.** Requests from a chat
  cloned or created inside the tracked code are not counted; check `n_calls`.
- **Routing is invisible.** A request sent through OpenRouter is estimated
  as if the model's own provider served it from its usual datacenter.

## Where next

- `carbon_run()` and `carbon_step()` accept the same tracker for expressions
  and pipelines; collect a pipeline's log with `carbon_collect()`.
- `carbon_tokens()` summarises a calls table's token use: tokens sent and
  received, cache hit rate and average context size.
- To estimate a Claude Code session, see `calls_from_transcript()`.
